RAW-B-010.why: The page records the upper bounds of Bleicher–Erdős, Yokota and Liu–Sawhney for general b. For prime b it records only the lower bound D(p) ≫ p log p, so it has no prime-specific construction. Check whether the upper-bound constructions behave differently at prime denominators.
RAW-B-010.first_step: Read Yokota [Yo88] and Liu–Sawhney [LiSa24] from the page; check whether their constructions treat prime b specially, and test the construction at targets 4/p.

RAW-B-012.why: Problem 307 asks for finite prime sets P,Q with (Σ1/p)(Σ1/q)=1. Cambie's examples exist only for the weakened, relatively-coprime version. The coprimality and product constraints may suggest parametrizations or obstructions for ES denominators.

RAW-B-016.why: The page reports Tang's upper bound δ(N) ≤ exp(−cN/(log N·log log N)³), i.e. very close near-misses to 1 exist; the trivial lower bound is 1/lcm(1..N). This calibrates how close reciprocal subset sums can come to a target, which is relevant to near-miss ES searches.

RAW-B-018.why: Problem 313 asks about 1/p_1+…+1/p_k = 1 − 1/m with distinct primes p_i (forcing m = p_1⋯p_k; primary pseudoperfect numbers). This is a close arithmetic cousin of fixed-term Egyptian fractions and may suggest product/divisor identities.

RAW-B-019.why: Lim–Steinerberger show that consecutive harmonic sums Σ_{n≤k≤m}1/k can exceed 1 by as little as ≪ n^{-2}(log n)^{-5/4+δ} for infinitely many n. This calibrates how closely structured reciprocal sums can approach a target, which bears on ES's fixed three-term constraint.

RAW-B-022.connection: Problem 317 ↔ ES F04, F12, F21, F27 (flip): small nonzero signed sums Σδ_k/k with δ_k∈{−1,0,1}, contrasted with ES's positive three-term sums.
RAW-B-022.why: Problem 317 asks how small a nonzero signed reciprocal sum can be, and whether it always exceeds 1/lcm(1..n) for large n. Such bounds may help rule out near-miss ES rational identities or control denominator sizes.

RAW-B-033.why: The page records upper bounds for D(b) for general b and the lower bound D(p) ≫ p log p at primes. Check whether any step of the constructions separates prime residue classes, since p≡1 mod 4 is the hard ES case.
RAW-B-033.first_step: Check whether the Bleicher–Erdős lower-bound argument for primes or the Yokota/Liu–Sawhney upper bounds distinguish p mod 4; if so, try adapting the hardest residue case to 4/p.

RAW-B-034.why: Croot's result shows that for large N every integer up to about H_N − (9/2+o(1))(log log N)²/log N is a sum of distinct 1/n with n ≤ N, and that this fails a little below H_N. Isolating this threshold mechanism may suggest how to handle finite exceptional sets in ES.

RAW-B-036.why: Tang's result is an upper bound for δ(N): it shows that very close near-misses exist, and the only lower bound is the trivial 1/lcm(1..N). Comparing this with ES near-misses (partial sums close to 4/p) may convert near-miss structure into divisor constraints.
RAW-B-036.first_step: After choosing x in ES, compare the size of the nonzero residual 4/p−1/x−1/y (trivially ≥ 1/(pxy)) with Tang's near-miss scale; derive the induced interval for the divisor parameter in the two-term completion.

RAW-B-045.why: The page records Vose's improvement N(b) ≪ √(log b) for the number of terms (not denominator size). The contrast between term-count bounds and ES's fixed three terms can benchmark certificate-size questions.
RAW-B-045.first_step: Read Vose [Vo85] and identify how denominators grow in his construction; compare with the polynomial-in-p size of any three-term ES certificate.

RAW-B-059.why: The page notes that the prime version of 307 forces |P∪Q| ≥ 60 and that only the relatively-coprime weakened version has known examples (Cambie). These exact reciprocal relations may expose congruence-covering patterns for selecting ES denominators.
RAW-B-059.first_step: Check Cambie's coprime examples on the page modulo 4 and 8; formulate a finite congruence-covering search for an ES denominator triple.

RAW-C-009.why: It is a verified explicit warning that rational density and local solubility do not settle an integral-point problem on a surface. The obstruction there is Brauer–Manin, which Bright–Loughran (arXiv:1908.02526) show is absent for ES, so look for non-BM ingredients.

RAW-C-032.first_step: Extract its parity rules and check whether one rewrite preserves the 2-adic valuation pattern of the denominators in known ES triples (e.g. 4/7 = 1/2+1/21+1/42 has no denominator divisible by 4).

RAW-C-035.connection: The two-for-two rewriting operator of arXiv:2003.13229 acts on unit-fraction decompositions, matching ES F12/F14/F27; it can be used to probe the term-count transition (two terms fail, three conjecturally suffice).
RAW-C-035.why: The paper itself proves no two-term obstruction theorem. Applying its rewrite to ES pairs may still show which arithmetic freedom the third ES denominator supplies.

RAW-C-038.why: A descent involution is a concrete way to reduce an infinite search to canonical roots. The ES equation (4x−p)yz = px(y+z) is degree 1 in each denominator, so there is no literal Vieta root swap. The available involutions are y↔z and the fibrewise divisor swap d↔p²x²/d on (ay−b)(az−b)=b² with a=4x−p, b=px.
RAW-C-038.first_step: Write the fixed-x fibre as (ay−b)(az−b)=b² with a=4x−p, b=px. Compose the divisor swap with the coordinate permutations and check integrality and positivity. Then check whether some height decreases outside a finite base set, as in the Markoff tree.

RAW-C-047.connection: Soundararajan's theorem (arXiv:0707.0299) shows that y-smooth integers below x are equidistributed in reduced residue classes mod q for q < y^{4√e−ε}. This matches ES F10/F20/F21, while ES needs a pointwise tied divisor.

RAW-a-006.connection: The divisor-sum formulation shares F10, F15, F21, F29: an ES witness exists iff a p-tied integer has a divisor in a prescribed residue class (this sub-problem is open, not solved).
